## Step 1: Explain the script

```{.r code-line-numbers="false"}
# Map recorded damage to property (méfait) in Montreal in 2025. # <1>
```

1. Explain that the script maps recorded damage to property, known as méfait in the source data, in Montreal in 2025. This identifies the task without requiring us to read the rest of the script. See [Organising code with comments](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/05_your_second_crime_map/index.html#sec-comments).

## Step 2: Load packages

```{.r code-line-numbers="false"}
# Load the packages needed for downloading, preparing and mapping the data
pacman::p_load(here, httr2, sf, sfhotspot, tidyverse) # <2>
```

2. `pacman::p_load()` loads the packages needed for this analysis, listed in alphabetical order with the tidyverse package last. **[here](https://here.r-lib.org/)** allows us to specify where to find files in the workspace; **[httr2](https://httr2.r-lib.org)** downloads data from the internet; **[sf](https://r-spatial.github.io/sf/)** handles spatial objects; **[sfhotspot](https://pkgs.lesscrime.info/sfhotspot/)** creates crime maps and estimates density; **[tidyverse](https://tidyverse.tidyverse.org)** provides tools for reading, wrangling and plotting data. Loading packages at the start makes it easy to check which tools the script needs. See [Loading packages](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/02_your_first_crime_map/index.html#sec-loading-packages).

## Step 3: Download the original data

```{.r code-line-numbers="false"}
# Download the original compressed CSV file and keep a local copy
request("https://mpjashby.github.io/crimemappingdata/montreal_mefait.csv.gz") |> # <3>
  # Save the file in the workspace's data/raw folder
  req_perform(path = here("data", "raw", "montreal_mefait.csv.gz")) # <4>
```

3. `request()` specifies the URL of the file to download. The pipe operator (`|>`) passes that request to the next function. The downloaded file is a compressed CSV (`.csv.gz`). We can read this format directly with `read_csv()`, so there is no need to extract it first. See [Downloading and loading data](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/02_your_first_crime_map/index.html#sec-load-data); [Stringing functions together](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/04_transforming_data/index.html#sec-pipe-operator).
4. `req_perform()` performs the download that was set up by `request()`. `here()` specifies where the original file should be saved, relative to the `crime_mapping` workspace. Keeping the original data in `data/raw` means we can return to it if we make a mistake while wrangling the data. See [Keeping your files organised](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/01_getting_started/index.html#sec-create-project).

## Step 4: Load and prepare the incidents

```{.r code-line-numbers="false"}
# Locate the downloaded file within the workspace
mefait_2025 <- here("data", "raw", "montreal_mefait.csv.gz") |> # <5>
  # Read the compressed CSV file, including its date column
  read_csv() |> # <6>
  # Convert column names to snake_case
  janitor::clean_names() |> # <7>
  # Keep dates from 1 January to 31 December 2025 inclusive
  filter(date >= ymd("2025-01-01"), date <= ymd("2025-12-31")) |> # <8>
  # Interpret x and y as projected coordinates in metres using EPSG:2950
  st_as_sf(coords = c("x", "y"), crs = "EPSG:2950") # <9>
```

5. `here()` specifies the location of the downloaded file. `<-` stores the result of the whole pipeline as `mefait_2025`, so the name reminds us which year the object contains. See [Keeping your files organised](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/01_getting_started/index.html#sec-create-project); [Naming objects](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/03_data_wrangling/index.html#sec-naming-objects); [Stringing functions together](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/04_transforming_data/index.html#sec-pipe-operator).
6. `read_csv()` from [readr](https://readr.tidyverse.org) reads the compressed CSV file and recognises its `date` column as dates. See [Loading CSV data](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/03_data_wrangling/index.html#sec-data-wrangling-loading-csv-data).
7. `janitor::clean_names()` from [janitor](https://sfirke.github.io/janitor/) converts column names to `snake_case`. Using `::` allows us to use this function without loading the whole package. See [Cleaning column names](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/05_your_second_crime_map/index.html#sec-your-second-crime-map-cleaning-column-names); [Loading packages](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/02_your_first_crime_map/index.html#sec-loading-packages).
8. `filter()` from [dplyr](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org) keeps dates on or after 1 January 2025 and on or before 31 December 2025. Both conditions must be satisfied. `ymd()` from [lubridate](https://lubridate.tidyverse.org) converts the text into dates. The file covers several years, but every row already relates to méfait, so only the year needs filtering. See [Filtering rows](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/03_data_wrangling/index.html#sec-filter-data).
9. `st_as_sf()` converts an ordinary object into a spatial object which specifies how the coordinates in the data correspond to locations of the earth. The argument `coords = c("x", "y")` specifies that the numeric coordinates describing each location are stored in the columns `x` and `y`. The argument `crs = "EPSG:2950"` describes how those coordaintes relate to places on the Earth's surface. Note that we know which code to use for the `crs` argument because that was specified in the exercise instructions. See [Converting data to an SF object](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/05_your_second_crime_map/index.html#sec-your-second-crime-map-converting-our-data-to-an-sf-object).


## Step 5: Draw the map

```{.r code-line-numbers="false"}
# Draw a point map over a base map, with small, partly transparent points
hotspot_map( # <10>
  mefait_2025, # <11>
  basemap_type = "cartolight", # <12>
  alpha = 0.25, # <13>
  colour = "blue2", # <14>
  size = 0.5 # <15>
)
```

10. `hotspot_map()` draws the spatial points over a base map. The arguments below then control how the points appear. Note that the result of this function is not stored in an object using `<-`, so running it causes the result (in this case, the map) to be displayed directly on the screen. See [Drawing the map](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/02_your_first_crime_map/index.html#sec-drawing-first-map).
11. Base the map on the 2025 data object created in the previous step.
12. Choose the light `cartolight` style of base map to provide local context without visually competing with the points showing damage to property. See [Base maps](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/07_map_context/index.html#sec-base-maps).
13. There are many crimes to show, so points may overlap. `alpha = 0.25` makes them partly transparent so that areas containing more overlapping points appear more prominent (although we will several better ways to solve this problem). See [Controlling aesthetics](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/05_your_second_crime_map/index.html#sec-aesthetics).
14. Blue points contrast with the light background. The incidents should stand out more than the features shown on the base map. See [Visual hierarchy](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/07_map_context/index.html#sec-visual-hierarchy).
15. Use small points with `size = 0.5` so that nearby incidents do not obscure one another as much.
